messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kofi's Story

Kofi was fifty years old and had been a plumber for thirty-two years—the kind of tradesman who took pride in solving problems others couldn't, who had built a reputation across his neighborhood for showing up on time and doing the work right. Three years ago, in the parking lot behind a commercial building where he'd gone to fix a burst pipe, a man had come at him with a knife. Kofi remembered almost nothing of it in words. What remained were images—the sudden shadow crossing the asphalt, the glint of the blade catching afternoon light, the man's face twisted in rage, and then the burning in his side as the knife went in. He'd fought back, managed to drive the man off, had been treated at the hospital and released. The police had taken a statement. Nothing had come of it. The man was never found. No arrest, no charges, no resolution. When Kofi tried to explain it to people, the words would tangle and slip away; the event existed in his mind as a series of vivid, fragmented pictures that he couldn't quite stitch together into a coherent account.

For months afterward, Kofi had tried to return to work as normal. But the assault had fundamentally altered what he believed about himself. He was no longer capable—not in the way he had been. The confidence that had carried him through three decades of work had cracked. He couldn't trust his own judgment anymore, couldn't be certain he would do the right thing in a moment of crisis. What if he froze next time? What if he wasn't quick enough? The injustice of it gnawed at him constantly. A man had tried to kill him, had scarred his abdomen and his psyche, and walked free. The police had done nothing. The world had simply moved on. This sense of profound unfairness, of being wronged without recourse, had seeped into how Kofi saw himself and his place in the world—he had come to believe that he was diminished, that the person he'd been before was gone, replaced by someone smaller and more fragile.

This shift in how Kofi understood himself fed directly into a narrowing of where he felt safe. His home became his refuge. His bedroom, even more so. Anywhere else—job sites, the grocery store, the street—felt permeable and dangerous. He began to turn down jobs that took him to unfamiliar locations. His wife, Ama, noticed him checking the locks repeatedly, positioning himself with his back to walls, tensing whenever a car door slammed outside. The threat felt constant and imminent, even though the rational part of him knew the risk was statistically small. What he had come to believe about his own vulnerability, his new incapacity, his helplessness in the face of an indifferent system, made the world feel inherently unsafe. He could not trust it, and he could not trust himself to navigate it.

The memories, too, pulled him back into that parking lot again and again. When Kofi lay in bed at night—which was most nights, because sleep had become nearly impossible—the images would come unbidden: the blade, the blood on his shirt, the face of his attacker. Each time they surfaced, they brought with them a crushing wave of guilt. He had been trained to handle emergencies, to stay calm and think clearly. Why hadn't he seen the man coming? Why hadn't he fought harder, faster? The guilt was irrational, he knew, but it clung to him. And those intrusive images, vivid and wordless, seemed to prove to him that the threat was real, ongoing, unforgotten by his body even if his mind wanted to move past it. The memories kept the danger alive in a way that transcended logic. He couldn't put the event into language that would contain it or make it manageable; it remained a series of visual shocks that bypassed thought altogether and went straight to his nervous system, triggering the same alarm response he'd felt in the parking lot.

Over time, Kofi had withdrawn further. He'd taken early retirement from his plumbing business, handing it over to a younger partner. He spent most days at home. His marriage, once warm and steady, had become strained by his emotional distance and his need to control their environment. Ama wanted him to see someone, to get help. For months, he'd resisted. But the isolation was becoming unbearable, and the sleep deprivation was catching up with him. He was exhausted, haunted, and afraid—not just of the world outside, but of what he'd become. Last week, he finally called a therapist. He didn't know if anything could fix this, if he could ever be the man he'd been before. But he was desperate enough now to try.
